teaser: A painter looks at you the way only Christ was allowed to. He meant it.
review_notes:
Image matches the listed work (date 1500, AD monogram and Latin inscription visible).
Silverpoint self-portrait at age 13 (1484, Albertina); painted self-portraits of 1493 (Louvre) and 1498 (Prado).
Inscription: 'Albertus Durerus Noricus ipsum me propriis sic effingebam coloribus aetatis anno XXVIII'. 'propriis' is translated here as 'my own'; some translate 'everlasting' or 'appropriate'.
Fur trim usually described as marten, a fur that Nuremberg dress rules reserved for the upper ranks: commonly stated, check.
Monogram AD also readable as Anno Domini: a frequent observation, not a documented intention.
Marcantonio Raimondi copying Dürer's prints with the monogram in Venice around 1506 and Dürer's complaint: from Vasari, details debated.
Bellini and the brush anecdote: told by Joachim Camerarius in 1532.
Panel kept in Nuremberg town hall; story of the painter Abraham Wolfgang Küfner sawing the panel to return a copy (around 1799) is traditional; acquired for the Bavarian royal collection in 1805.
Oil on limewood, about 67 x 49 cm.
No independent painted self-portrait after 1500: he later appears only as a small figure in larger pictures.

lesson.text: Thirteen. That is how old Albrecht Dürer was when he first drew his own face, with a mirror and a metal point, in his father's goldsmith shop in Nuremberg. Almost nobody did that in 1484. He painted himself again at 21 and at 26. Then, at 28, he made this one, and went further than anyone before him.

By then he had reason to be confident. Two years earlier he had published a book of large prints of the Apocalypse, the end of the world as told in the Bible, and it had sold all over Europe. Prints travel in a way paintings cannot. A craftsman's son from a German trading town was becoming the most famous artist north of the Alps.

Portraits of the time turned the sitter slightly to one side, the three-quarter view. A face shown dead straight, perfectly symmetrical, on a dark ground, was something people knew from one kind of picture only: the image of Christ. Dürer builds his own face on that model, and you can measure it.
Three lines that turn a face into an icon, a holy image.

lines.label: The axis
lines.text: Hair parting, nose, the middle of the lips, the opening of the coat: all stacked on one vertical in the exact center of the panel.

lines.label: The triangle
lines.text: The hair falls from the crown to the shoulders in two equal slopes. Head and curls form a triangle, the most stable shape there is.

lines.label: The eyes
lines.text: Both eyes sit on one level line and look straight ahead. Wherever you stand, they are on you.

lesson.text: Was he claiming to be Christ? Probably not. Christians were urged to live in imitation of Christ, and Dürer took that literally with a brush. He also believed, as he wrote later, that an artist's power to create comes from God. The picture says both things at once: I follow him, and my gift is from him.
In 1500, Dürer gives a painter's face the format reserved for the holiest image. It is one of the first times an artist presents himself as more than a craftsman.

He does not leave it to the face alone. The dark background carries two pieces of gold writing, placed level with his eyes like captions, and lower down his own right hand enters the picture. Each of them adds a line to the argument.
Read the painting the way Dürer wrote it: left, right, then down.

spots.title: 1500 and AD
spots.text: The year, and under it his monogram: a D tucked between the legs of a large A. They are his initials. They are also the letters of Anno Domini, “in the year of the Lord”.

spots.title: The Latin lines
spots.text: Four lines in Latin, the language of scholars: “I, Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg, painted myself thus in my own colors, at the age of twenty-eight.”

spots.title: The hand
spots.text: Where Christ's hand would rise in blessing, Dürer's fingers touch the fur of his collar. It is the painter's working hand, the tool that made everything you see.

spots.title: The fur
spots.text: A wide collar of soft brown fur, painted tip by tip. Costly fur like this signaled high rank in Nuremberg. No painter's apron here: he dresses as a gentleman.

lesson.text: That monogram became one of the first artist's trademarks, and one of the first to be pirated. A few years later in Venice, an Italian engraver copied Dürer's prints line for line, AD included, and sold them. Dürer complained to the authorities.

The hair is a show of skill in itself. Each curl is built from separate strokes of light brown and gold over dark, so the locks catch the light like twisted wire. He worked in oil on a panel of limewood, about 67 by 49 centimeters (26 by 19 inches): smaller than most people expect, a little under life-size.

The Venetian master Giovanni Bellini is said to have asked Dürer for one of the special brushes he used to paint hair. Dürer handed him a few ordinary ones. Bellini did not believe him, so Dürer picked one up and painted a long wavy lock on the spot.

As far as we know, nobody ordered this picture and Dürer never sold it. It seems to have stayed with him, and later it hung in the town hall of Nuremberg, where the city showed it off as a relic of its greatest son. In 1805 it was sold to the Bavarian royal collection in Munich.

It nearly disappeared on the way. A persistent story says that around 1800 the city lent the panel to a local painter to copy. He sawed the wood in two through its thickness, glued his copy onto the back half with its official seals, returned that, and kept the real painting to sell.

After 1500, Dürer lived another 28 years and painted emperors, merchants and saints. He slipped his own small figure into the corner of several altarpieces. But he never again painted himself alone on a panel. Maybe there was nothing left to add.

quiz.question: What made the pose so daring in 1500?
options: A straight frontal view was the format of images of Christ
He painted himself without a hat
quiz.explanation: Ordinary portraits were three-quarter views; the frontal face belonged to Christ.

quiz.question: What does the Latin inscription say?
options: That Dürer painted himself in his own colors at twenty-eight
That the painting belongs to the city of Nuremberg
A prayer for the new century
quiz.explanation: It names him, his city and his age, and says he painted himself.

quiz.question: What else can the letters AD stand for?
quiz.explanation: His initials are also the abbreviation for “in the year of the Lord”.

quiz.question: What is Dürer's hand doing?
options: Touching the fur of his collar
quiz.explanation: His fingers rest on the fur where Christ's blessing hand would be.

quiz.question: What had already made Dürer famous by 1500?
quiz.explanation: His printed Apocalypse sold across Europe two years earlier.

facts.text: Dürer drew his first self-portrait at thirteen.
facts.explanation: He drew his face in his father's goldsmith shop in 1484.

facts.text: The portrait was commissioned by the emperor.
facts.explanation: As far as we know nobody ordered it, and Dürer kept it.

facts.text: Dürer went on to paint many more self-portraits like this one in old age.
facts.explanation: After 1500 he never again painted himself alone on a panel.
